title: Republican Bill Would Raise H-1B Exemption Threshold to Nearly $140,000
excerpt: House and Senate versions of the Protecting American Workers Through H-1B Modernization Act would replace the $60,000 salary exemption for H-1B-dependent employers, frozen since 1998, with twice the national average wage index — nearly $140,000 today.
body:
• Republican bills in the House and Senate would raise the salary exemption for H-1B-dependent employers from $60,000, set in 1998, to nearly $140,000 today.
  • The figure is not a minimum H-1B salary: it is the pay level at which a visa-dependent employer can skip recruitment and non-displacement attestations; workers paid less would trigger those attestations, and the master's-degree exemption would remain.
  • The new threshold would move automatically, set at twice the Social Security Administration's National Average Wage Index, which is now nearly $70,000.
  • Reader check: the proposal is not law, has no immediate effect on H-1B petitions or extensions, and the House bill, H.R. 10799, sits in the Judiciary Committee with the House out until after the November 3 midterms.

Republican lawmakers have introduced legislation in both chambers of Congress that would raise a key H-1B salary threshold from $60,000 to nearly $140,000, tightening the conditions under which companies that rely heavily on the visa can hire more foreign workers without first recruiting Americans. The Protecting American Workers Through H-1B Modernization Act would replace the fixed $60,000 figure, unchanged since 1998, with a formula tied to national wage growth. Senator Jon Husted of Ohio introduced the Senate version, S. 5638, on September 30, and Representative Glenn Grothman of Wisconsin filed the House companion, H.R. 10799, on October 13, according to hi INDiA.

What the threshold does

Under current law, an employer whose H-1B workers make up more than a set share of its workforce is classed as H-1B-dependent. Such employers must attest that they have tried to recruit U.S. workers for a job and will not displace them. They are exempt from those attestations for a given hire if they pay the H-1B worker at least $60,000 a year, or if the worker holds a master's degree or higher. The bill targets only the salary route to that exemption. It would not set a minimum salary for H-1B workers in general, and it would not remove the master's-degree exemption.

The $60,000 figure was set in 1998, when it was intended to equal twice the Social Security Administration's National Average Wage Index. It has never been adjusted. That index is now nearly $70,000, so applying the original formula today produces a threshold of nearly $140,000, according to Husted's Senate office. The bill would write the formula into law, so the threshold would rise with wages instead of staying frozen until Congress acts again.

"For decades, companies have been able to sidestep hiring American workers because of a salary threshold that hasn't budged since 1998. That's not modernization, that's a loophole."

— Jon Husted, U.S. Senator for Ohio

Who would feel it

The sponsors describe the affected group as mostly IT outsourcing and staffing firms. Indian nationals receive the bulk of H-1B visas each year, and large Indian and Indian-origin IT services companies are among the employers most likely to be classified as H-1B-dependent, hi INDiA reported. For those firms, a hire below the new threshold would no longer be a paperwork shortcut: the employer would have to run the recruitment and non-displacement attestations that the exemption currently waives. That raises the cost and time involved in placing H-1B staff, even though the bill does not cap numbers or bar any hire outright.

Grothman made the same argument as his Senate counterpart. "American workers should come first in their own country," he said in a statement. "Employers should not be able to use a salary threshold established nearly three decades ago to bypass protections for qualified Americans."

Where the bill stands

The proposal is one of several H-1B measures moving at the same time. Representative Beth Van Duyne of Texas introduced H.R. 10643 on October 1 to raise penalties for wilful displacement of American workers to $250,000, and the administration has separately pursued H-1B changes through fees and rulemaking. A similar threshold idea cleared the House Judiciary Committee in 2017 before dying, a reminder that introduction is a procedural step, not a change to any rule.

For now, nothing changes for workers or employers. H.R. 10799 has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee, has no cosponsors yet, and the House is out until after the November 3 midterm elections, making movement before then unlikely. The bill must still pass both chambers and be signed before any employer faces the higher threshold.
